title: WEEKEND READING: From evidence to engagement: how to bring research and policy closer together?
summary:
This blog was kindly authored by Helen Tattam, SKOPE Visiting Policy Fellow, Department for Education, Xin Xu, Lecturer in Higher and Tertiary Education, Deputy Director of SKOPE, Gonzalo Hidalgo Bazan, Postdoctoral Researcher at SKOPE, James Robson, Director of Oxford University Centre on Skills, Knowledge and Organisational Performance (SKOPE) and Associate Professor of Tertiary Education Systems, […]

The post WEEKEND READING: From evidence to engagement: how to bring research and policy closer together? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Helen Tattam, SKOPE Visiting Policy Fellow, Department for Education, Xin Xu, Lecturer in Higher and Tertiary Education, Deputy Director of SKOPE, Gonzalo Hidalgo Bazan, Postdoctoral Researcher at SKOPE, James Robson, Director of Oxford University Centre on Skills, Knowledge and Organisational Performance (SKOPE) and Associate Professor of Tertiary Education Systems, Adam Saunders, Research Fellow at SKOPE, and Yushan Xie, SKOPE Research Officer.

How does research translate into policy impact?

There is a common myth that good research will eventually find its way into policy. It goes like this: researchers conduct rigorous studies, produce robust evidence, publish it well, disseminate a policy brief or two, and policymakers pick it up. Policy impact then follows.

In reality, things are rarely so straightforward.

Policy engagement is not an ‘end product’ of research

In reality, policy engagement is not a single output or a one-off event. The process itself is part of the engagement. Too often, it needs to begin before the research is even conducted. Policy engagement works best when it is routine rather than occasional, collective rather than purely individual, and strategic rather than reactive. It depends on relationships, translation, trust, and timing.

For researchers, that means treating policy engagement as something to begin earlier, sustain over time, and shape carefully around live policy contexts. For higher education institutions and policy actors, it means creating more spaces and structures that make this kind of exchange possible.

The reality of policymaking that researchers need to understand

People often talk about a ‘policy cycle’. In it which a problem is identified, evidence is gathered, options are developed, a decision is taken, implementation follows and evaluation comes after. However, policy rarely begins with a blank page and almost never unfolds so smoothly. This idealised ‘policy cycle’ model has its uses, but the reality of policymaking is much more complex and messier.

Policymaking is rarely linear. Instead, it is iterative and reactive, responding to changing circumstances and political priorities. It is more like a relay race. A policymaking opportunity takes a few steps, and then the baton is passed to the next window of opportunity, where a little more progress may be possible. Policymaking is shaped by time pressures, electoral cycles, budget limitations, media attention, crises, flagship manifesto commitments, institutional constraints and changes in political priority. Therefore, there are trade-offs to be made between developing sufficient evidence, maintaining a certain ideology that a government might be committed to, practical logistics and competing interests within parties, among key stakeholders and across the electorate. In this context, evidence matters, but politics and feasibility often matter more.

How does meaningful research-policy engagement happen?

Firstly, policymakers need actionable insights.

They need evidence that is concise, actionable, and feasible. They need to understand not just the nuance, but the practical significance. Academic rigour and policy utility are not always the same thing, but nor should they be treated as opposites. Policymaking needs rigorous research to understand what is happening, why it matters, how different stakeholder perspectives come into play, and what alternatives might be the most effective next steps.

In fast-moving policy environments, researchers also need to communicate the ‘so what’ clearly. Storytelling, real-world examples, diagrams, infographics, or a strong headline statistic can all help research to travel more effectively in policy settings.

Secondly, strategic relationship building matters.

Meaningful engagement needs structures and routines that build trust and that support ongoing discussion, planning, and collaboration. If researchers are building relationships with civil servants and other intermediaries at different levels, and are thinking together about shared areas of interest over time, they are better placed to recognise and respond to windows of opportunity when they arise.

However, everyone has limited time and energy. Although there is a real appetite for collaboration within the civil service, in practice engagement often depends on individual connections or short-term funding arrangements, making it personal, uneven, and hard to sustain.

Therefore, it is important to move beyond an arm’s-length model, in which researchers are positioned only as consultants, sounding boards, or technical experts at isolated moments. More strategic and institutional relationship building will help to lead to durable research-policy engagement.

Finally, relationship-based engagement raises important questions about capacity, access, and equity.

The time, networks, and institutional support needed to build these connections are unevenly distributed across the higher education sector. Therefore, it is important to think about how policy engagement can be supported in ways that broaden access, rather than reinforce existing inequalities between individuals and institutions.

Learning from practice: what sustained research–policy engagement can look like

At SKOPE, we have explored how research and policy can be brought together around a shared agenda on tertiary education and the skills system in England. This involved convening workshops, roundtables, and larger events that brought together academics, policymakers, employers, and other stakeholders. The aim was not simply to share research, but to test ideas, surface practical challenges, connect evidence to live policy questions and explore different and sometimes competing perspectives on reform.

Several lessons stood out to us through this process.

Firstly, acting as a neutral convenor can enable more open and constructive discussion, particularly on complex or contested issues. Higher education institutions are often well placed to play this role. Bringing together participants across departments and sectors can also help address the fragmentation that often limits policymaking, enabling more joined-up conversations on cross-cutting challenges.

Secondly, co-development is equally important. Engagement is more effective when researchers and policymakers shape questions, activities and outputs together, rather than working in sequence. Sustained interaction over time allows trust, shared understanding, and responsiveness to develop, making it easier to recognise and act on emerging policy opportunities. It also helps build a more collective understanding of both the challenges and the realistic pathways for reform.

A further lesson was the importance of intentionality in how engagement is designed. Individual workshops, roundtables, or meetings should not be treated as discrete events, but as part of a wider process of building a shared agenda. Without this continuity, even high-quality discussions can dissipate without leading to further collaboration, insight, or impact. Structuring engagement with clear follow-on pathways, whether through ongoing dialogue, co-produced outputs, or future activities, is therefore critical to converting exchange into progress.

Structured mechanisms such as fellowships, secondments, and institutional partnerships can play a critical role in enabling this kind of engagement. By creating protected time, space, and continuity, they allow relationships to deepen and move beyond one-off or transactional interactions. These conditions, such as institutional support, dedicated time, and sustained contact, are relatively simple in principle but often scarce in practice. Without them, engagement risks remaining ad hoc and uneven.

While the example of our work reflects a particular context, the implications of it are wider. Effective research-policy engagement is not just about better dissemination. It is about creating the conditions for ongoing, collaborative relationships in which evidence, perspectives, and policy can evolve together, and where voices that are overlooked or separated out in policy debates can be represented and brought together.

title: Is Burnham’s Oxbridge-heavy cabinet a sign of social mobility or lack of progress on class?
summary:

full_text:
Like 20 British prime ministers before him, Andy Burnham’s new cabinet minister for AI, Kanishka Narayan, went to Eton. After graduating from the country’s most elite private school, Narayan attended Balliol College, Oxford, where he studied – what else? – PPE (politics, philosophy and economics), like David Cameron, Rishi Sunak, Ed Miliband and a host of other senior politicians. An MBA at Stanford and a career in the City followed.

But Narayan’s background is hardly typical of the British ruling class. Born in Bihar in eastern India, he moved with his family to Cardiff when he was 12. He and his younger brother were sleeping on the floor of their one-bedroom home when a teacher at his local high school suggested the bright young boy apply for some private schools. His parents, who had joined the Labour party almost as soon as they arrived in Wales, ran a petrol station. Eton was possible only thanks to a full scholarship.

Class and representation in 21st-century Britain can be complicated. By some yardsticks, for example, the makeup of Burnham’s ministerial team, which was announced after he became prime minister on Monday, could be seen as a backward step. More than a fifth of his cabinet attended private schools for most of their education – at times, under Keir Starmer, every senior minister went to a state school. And a remarkable 54% of the ministers now leading government policy went to Oxford or Cambridge, up from 29% under Starmer. (Nationally, the figure is 1%.)

In other ways, however, Burnham’s top team is more diverse than before, with half of those attending cabinet – including, of course, the PM – representing northern constituencies. And for the first time in history, the cabinet has equal numbers of women and men. One of them, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is among those who were educated privately – this after she and her family arrived in Britain as asylum seekers from Liberia in 1986.

How much does all of this matter? The prime minister’s top ministers ought to be competent – do they need to be representative too?

To Nick Harrison, the chief executive of the Sutton Trust, which works to promote social mobility, the answer is an emphatic yes. “Of course, the background of the cabinet matters. If they’re meant to be representing the country, they should be representative of the country. We would absolutely say that you get better decisions if you have a wide range of views, perspectives and backgrounds around the table.”

The sample size of 28 cabinet attendees may be small, but to Sam Friedman, a professor of sociology at London School of Economics whose work focuses on class and inequality, its makeup is symbolic of the wider access to power in Britain. Scrutinising those in senior positions “provides a window into a wider conversation about how people’s backgrounds shape their ability to reach the top positions in our society”, he says.

Power in Britain remains overwhelmingly concentrated in the hands of a very narrow group of people, according to Friedman’s research. He points out that pupils of the nine most exclusive private schools are still, today, 52 times more likely to reach elite positions than those who go to any other type of school. Oxbridge graduates born in the 1960s and early 1970s – Burnham was born in 1970 and went to Cambridge – were more than 250 times more likely to reach the British elite than their peers who did not go to university.

The cabinet – whatever its makeup – is merely the visible tip of a vast iceberg of powerbrokers, whose own elite backgrounds can be key in the way government decisions are taken, argues Friedman. According to his own research surveying attitudes among the elite, he says “those who are brought up in more privileged backgrounds tend to tilt to the right”, and “people in positions of power in the cabinet are often interacting with civil servants and business leaders who mediate their ability” to take decisions.

To Lee Elliot Major, a professor of social mobility at the University of Exeter, it is legitimate to scrutinise the backgrounds of those running the country, but “counting private schools and Oxbridge degrees only tells part of the story. The real challenge is whether ministers understand how Britain’s contemporary opportunity system now works.

“Traditional markers such as school attended or parents’ occupations no longer signal advantage in the straightforward way they once did. Today’s divides are increasingly shaped by wealth, place, networks and the hidden cultural codes that govern entry and progression into our elites.”

The challenge goes way beyond widening access to the traditional routes to power, important though that may be, Major argues. Instead, politicians of whatever background must grapple what he calls “the profound unravelling of the promise of modern capitalism” – the fact that, for people in their 40s and younger, there are now more people experiencing downward mobility than upward, meaning they are less well-off than their parents.

“The test for this government isn’t whether ministers themselves are socially mobile. It’s whether they can create a society in which many more people have genuine opportunities to flourish,” Major says.

Dr Daniel Evans, a lecturer at Swansea University whose work includes a focus on politics and social class, agrees. “The origin story [of politicians] is a bit of a red herring,” he says. “The bigger story is the total collapse of the graduate premium and the debt that students are getting into in university and how brutal the job market is for graduates.

“We keep talking about social mobility as if everyone can do it, but university is out of reach for loads of people financially, the job market is horrendous. No one can get a flat. The discourse hasn’t kept up.”

title: How Trump Accounts could impact your child's student aid
full_text:
Touted as an "IRA for children," Trump Accounts promise to give your child a "head start on the American Dream."

These tax-advantaged investment accounts come with a one-time $1,000 contribution from the federal government. When your child turns 18, the money can be used for their education, a home purchase, or other qualified expenses.

However, questions remain about how these accounts factor into financial aid formulas. Here's what we know.

Trump Accounts, explained

Trump Accounts, created under President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, are tax-deferred investment accounts for Americans under age 18.

The goal: Bolster the next generation by giving children a head start on their wealth-building journey, so that they later can afford to buy a home, retire early, fund their education, and more. "Trump Accounts are now live, giving every child a stake in the American Dream from day one, thanks to President Trump," said U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement.

As the child grows, additional contributions of up to $5,000, including $2,500 from employers, can be made by parents, family members, employers, and other organizations along the way. Those born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, get the added incentive of a one-time contribution of $1,000 from the government.

These accounts are technically owned by the child but managed by a parent or custodian until that child turns 18 — right around the time most people head to college. Withdrawals are generally subject to ordinary income tax.

According to the White House Council of Economic Advisers, account balances can reach a minimum of $5,800 with no additional contributions or a maximum of $303,800 by age 18 if maximum contributions are made, assuming average returns on the US stock market.

For many parents, this may seem like a no-brainer; however, the Department of Education hasn't released any official information as to how Trump Accounts will factor into need-based aid.

Read more: The overlooked group Melania Trump helped add to Trump Accounts

How Trump Accounts may play a role in college aid

The Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) assesses your eligibility for student aid, including federal grants, student loans, and work-study programs. To determine your eligibility, it considers the cost of attendance (COA) for a particular school and the Student Aid Index (SAI).

The Student Aid Index considers a family's financial resources, including parent and student assets, income, and living expenses, to determine how much they can contribute toward college costs.

Experts argue that Trump Accounts could create a hurdle for students in the future by potentially reducing the amount of aid they qualify for if these accounts are treated as student assets, which are assessed at a higher rate than parent assets.

"Financial aid measures two things — income and assets. My understanding is that the Trump Account will be an asset of the student, which can reduce aid by as much as 20 cents on every dollar in the account," said Jack Wang, wealth advisor at Innovative Advisory Group and host of the "Smart College Buyer" podcast.

Wang notes that withdrawals could have additional implications on financial aid eligibility. "Once money is withdrawn from the account, that can count as income to the student, which can reduce aid by as much as 50 cents on the dollar."

This differs from parent-owned 529 plans, which are treated as parent assets and assessed at a more favorable maximum rate of 5.64%.

Is a Trump Account the right move for your child?

The $1,000 injection into Trump Accounts for those who qualify is a big bonus, and can certainly make a difference for many families — but there are other account options available that could prove to be more beneficial long-term if your goal is to fund higher education.

For example, 529 plans may not offer the $1,000 seed money, but they offer tax-free withdrawals for qualified education expenses and higher annual contribution limits.

When choosing a savings vehicle for higher education, it's important to consider how the account you choose will grow with your child, contribution caps, tax implications, and financial aid implications to determine if it's the right fit for your financial plan.

"The general advice is that if a family has a newborn and can get the $1,000 starter deposit, that is worth doing," said Wang. "Whether the family should continue to save in that account is a different question entirely. If a family anticipates need-based federal aid, and they aren't going to get the initial deposit bonus, then there may be better options than a Trump Account."

title: Each Student Has a Different Door: What I Learned About Learning Styles from Andrew Cohen — and from My Own Students
summary:
After attending a summer workshop on learning strategies led by Professor Andrew Cohen, I returned to my Spanish classrooms at Northwestern University with a simple question: What would happen if my students became aware of how they learned?  To explore this, I introduced an anonymous learning strategies survey that I had adapted from one I had […]

The post Each Student Has a Different Door: What I Learned About Learning Styles from Andrew Cohen — and from My Own Students appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
After attending a summer workshop on learning strategies led by Professor Andrew Cohen, I returned to my Spanish classrooms at Northwestern University with a simple question: What would happen if my students became aware of how they learned?

To explore this, I introduced an anonymous learning strategies survey that I had adapted from one I had learned during the workshop (https://tinyurl.com/2j39ka6m). I explained that their honest responses would help me support their learning and asked them to complete it at home so they could reflect honestly. The next day, to ensure anonymity, I asked students to place their completed surveys into an envelope and stepped out of the room while they submitted them. This small gesture encouraged openness and trust.

The survey asked students to reflect on their listening, vocabulary, speaking, reading, and writing. The goal was not to evaluate them, but to help them understand their own learning.

Their responses transformed my teaching. For the first time, I saw the diversity of learning strategies in my classroom. Some relied on memorization, even when it was ineffective. Others described strategies such as listening to music, visualizing words, or repeating phrases aloud. Several students said they had never been asked to reflect on how they learned. They began to realize their difficulties did not reflect lack of ability, but a mismatch between how they studied and how they learned best.

Based on what I learned, I made small but meaningful changes, encouraging students to use visual flashcards, personal writing, music, and oral repetition to support their learning.

The classroom environment also shifted. Students became more confident and patient with themselves and others. Learning was no longer an isolated struggle, but a shared process.

Looking back, this survey produced three important outcomes: greater metacognitive awareness, more responsive instruction, and increased learner autonomy.

Around this time, I encountered the Integrated Performance Assessment (IPA) model developed by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages (ACTFL), which organizes language learning into interpretive, interpersonal, and presentational modes. This framework was important because it gave structure to what I had begun to see: language learning happens through multiple forms of engagement, and each student enters through a different door.

In the end, my students were not only learning Spanish. They were teaching me how learning happens.

Practical Takeaway: Invite Students to Reflect on Their Learning

Instructors can build on a learning strategies survey by:

Asking students to discuss which strategies work best for them

Encouraging students to experiment with new approaches

Designing activities that include listening, speaking, reading, and writing

Normalizing the idea that learners use different pathways

These conversations help students become more confident, independent, and engaged.

When Students Teach the Teacher

As I read my students’ surveys, I began to realize that many had never been asked how they learned. They had been graded and corrected but rarely invited to reflect on their learning processes.

Their answers were revealing. One student needed repetition. Another relied on writing by hand. Another used visualization and personal associations. Their challenges were not about effort, but alignment between teaching and learning.

And this realization changed how I taught—and how I listened. I began paying closer attention to how students approached learning. Their reflections helped me see patterns I had previously overlooked and reminded me that effective teaching begins with understanding the learner.

I introduced activities that allowed multiple entry points into the language, including music, personal writing, and oral practice. Students became more confident and willing to experiment. They began to see that there was not one correct way to learn.

In the same time, the IPA framework helped guide these instructional choices. Its emphasis on interpretive, interpersonal, and presentational communication allowed me to design activities that supported the diverse learning processes already present in my classroom. Instead of expecting all students to learn in the same way, I could help each of them engage with the language more effectively.

My students were not only learning Spanish. They were teaching me how to teach.

Practical Takeaway: Align Instruction with How Students Learn

Instructors can build on student strategy awareness by:

Asking students to share which learning techniques help them most

Offering options for practice, such as visual, written, and oral activities

Encouraging students to experiment and reflect on what works

Adjusting instruction based on student feedback

When instruction aligns with how students learn, engagement and confidence increase.

Listening to My Students: What the Survey Revealed

One of the most revealing parts of the survey was not only how students learned, but why they were learning Spanish.

Their motivations were deeply personal. Some wanted to travel or advance professionally. Others wanted to communicate with people they loved. I still remember the laughter when one student said, “My girlfriend is from Colombia. I need to speak with her family.” Another said simply, “My boyfriend is from Spain. I don’t want translation to be part of our relationship.” In that moment, language was not an assignment. It was a bridge.

The survey also helped students recognize their strengths. Many discovered they were visual learners and began using images and flashcards. Others relied on repetition, writing, or meaningful communication. As students became more aware of how they learned, their confidence grew.

Years later, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I carried this lesson into a different classroom while I volunteered to teach Hebrew on Zoom to students across Latin America and the United States. Many were learning Hebrew as part of a personal journey of identity and connection.

Remembering my earlier experience, I invited them to reflect on how they learned. Their responses were familiar, but my role had changed. I was no longer discovering their differences for the first time. I was listening to them intentionally.

In the end, I learned something essential: Teaching begins with listening.

And the question that continues to guide me is simple: How can we help students discover how they learn?

Practical Takeaways for Instructors

Instructors can apply this approach by:

Asking students how they learn

Using anonymous surveys or reflective discussions

Offering multiple ways to practice and engage

Encouraging students to experiment with strategies

Even small conversations about learning can transform student confidence and engagement.

Rifka Epstein is a language educator specializing in Spanish and Hebrew instruction, intercultural learning, and student identity. She taught for many years at Northwestern University and now lives in Beit Shemesh, Israel, where she continues teaching and writing.

title: Bringing education technology into focus
summary: As interactive displays, AV-over-IP, hybrid learning tools and connected classrooms are moving from pilot projects to core infrastructure, the people specifying and managing that technology are looking for somewhere to compare options, ask hard questions and learn from peers facing the same decisions. At Integrate 2026, from 2 to 4 September at ICC Sydney, we …
full_text:
As interactive displays, AV-over-IP, hybrid learning tools and connected classrooms are moving from pilot projects to core infrastructure, the people specifying and managing that technology are looking for somewhere to compare options, ask hard questions and learn from peers facing the same decisions.

At Integrate 2026, from 2 to 4 September at ICC Sydney, we are bringing together more than 120 exhibitors across 10 technology zones to do just that. For those professionals working in the higher education sector whose responsibilities cover AV, IT and learning environments, Integrate is the place to see how the technology reshaping campuses actually performs, side by side and in person.

A show floor built around learning spaces

A number of Integrate’s 10 technology zones speak directly to those working in tertiary environments.

Projection, Video and Interactive Displays showcases the screens and collaboration surfaces that are now standard in lecture theatres and flexible learning rooms.

UCC, Conferencing and Collaboration covers the platforms that support hybrid teaching and remote participation.

IT Networking and Software Solutions addresses the infrastructure that ties it all together.

Digital Signage and Audio Systems rounds out the tools that shape how information moves across a campus.

Rather than reading spec sheets, visitors can compare products from competing suppliers in one place, test them, and talk directly to the people who build and support them.

For institutions who often work with long procurement cycles and stakeholder sign-offs, that direct access shortens the distance between evaluating a solution and making the case for it internally.

The AETM connection

Integrate’s relationship with the education sector runs deep through its partnership with the Australian Education Technology Management association (AETM).

AETM is made up largely of educational technology managers, directors and IT professionals from universities and TAFE colleges across Australia and New Zealand. Its members are responsible for technology in teaching spaces that serve more than a million students.

That partnership takes a visible form through the AETM K-12 Conference, held on the first day of Integrate 2026. The half-day conference is a focused session on current AV education technologies and how they apply in classroom and learning environments, specifically within the K-12 school sector.

It brings together AV coordinators, IT managers and technology professionals from primary and secondary schools alongside product specialists and solution providers. The conference is a paid event, but free for AETM members.

While the K-12 Conference speaks to the school sector, it sits within a wider education programme at Integrate that reaches across both school and tertiary environments, giving professionals from every level of education a reason to attend.

Tech Talks: Education across three days

The Integrate and AVIXA Tech Talks run across all three days in the Tech Talks Theatre on the show floor. Developed in partnership with the Audiovisual and Integrated Experience Association (AVIXA), the programme looks at trends and their practical applications shaping today’s industry. Topics for 2026 include AI in AV, real-time video analysis, sustainability, hybrid workplace technology and live events.

For technology managers in higher education, the sessions offer the kind of structured, vendor-neutral learning that is usually only available through international travel.

The AI in AV sessions, in particular, reflect a question many campuses are working through right now: where does technology add real value in teaching and operations, and where does it not? The Tech Talks are a paid programme, with sessions available across the three days.

Recognising the next generation

Integrate also invests in the people who will build and manage the campuses of the future. The AVIXA Tech Crew, running on 4 September, gives secondary school students a one-day introduction to the AV industry, including a panel of young professionals sharing their career paths and a guided tour of the show floor. For educators thinking about pathways into technology careers, it is a practical example of the industry engaging with students directly.

Planning your visit

Entry to the Integrate 2026 show floor is free to register, and one registration also covers the co-located Security Exhibition and Conference and Fire Security Expo. The Tech Talks and the AETM K-12 Conference are paid programmes, though AETM members attend the K-12 Conference at no cost.

For university professionals, the value is in the concentration: 10 technology zones, more than 120 suppliers, a dedicated education programme and three days of learning in one venue.

Whether the goal is comparing interactive displays for a lecture theatre refresh, understanding AV-over-IP for a campus network, or staying abreast of the future of education technology, Integrate is a direct route to the answers.

Registration is open now at integrate-expo.com/register
